summary: Nova Scotia's tallest lighthouse, first lit in 1861 after the Hungarian wreck. Octagonal concrete tower of 1924; the lost Fresnel lens was found in 2018.

lens.note: Rediscovered in Saint John, N.B., in 2018.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Coast Guard list: 30.0 m structure. LighthouseFriends: 101 ft to the top. Lighthouse Directory: 31 m (101 ft). The 1924 report: 86 ft tower plus 10 ft lantern. The story gives about 30 m (101 ft) and gives the Lighthouse Directory's 31 m alongside it.
LighthouseFriends says the Friends raised more than $90,000 for the 2013 work. The Lighthouse Directory gives $95,000. Both give the province's $50,000. The story gives both figures.
Two Halifax dispatches in one paper disagree: one says the Hungarian left Liverpool on the 8th, the other that she sailed from Queenstown on the 9th. LighthouseFriends follows the Liverpool date.
Barrington dispatch: lights seen at four o'clock. Cape Sable message to Cunard: three o'clock on Monday morning. LighthouseFriends: about three. The story reports the disagreement.

LighthouseFriends: struck the cape on the night of 19 February 1860. The Barrington dispatch dated 20 February and the Monday-morning message put the lights early on 20 February. The story gives both.

notes_for_editor: Keepers are from the LighthouseFriends roster only. The Marine keeper tables for 1900 to 1908 list Isaac Doane and A. H. Cunningham among the Nova Scotia keepers, but the OCR columns do not tie either name to this station, so neither is linked by position. The LighthouseFriends roster has overlapping dates for Francis Casey and Andy Dugandzic (1982 to 1986 and 1984 to 1986). LighthouseFriends does not link Sidney F. Smith to the keeper's children of 1942; the story does not link them. The keeper's children and the keeper's household are not named in the story (private people who may be alive). The 1942 rescue rests on LighthouseFriends' account of the Smith family's recollections (it cites a 2011 article by Carl Anderson); uboat.net confirms only the sinking and its date. The Hungarian passenger count: LighthouseFriends gives 205. The agents' counts in New York, reprinted in the Biddeford paper of 23 March 1860, are too faint in the OCR to total. The Barrington keeper's light is not identified in the paper; it is not this station, and it is not identified as Baccaro Point in any source read here. LighthouseFriends repeats a legend about a diary ('Lizzie dies tonight'); it has no source and is not used. Searches of Chronicling America for 'Cape Sable' and 'light' in 1861 returned nothing. The Wikipedia article for the lighthouse returned 404 and is not used. The Directory of Federal Heritage Designations pages for the record's ID returned empty placeholders. The Marconi wireless station at Cape Sable (1905 to 1906, Marine report) is not placed relative to the light and is not used. The Clark's Harbour life-saving station is not this lighthouse; it is used only as a nearby station. Record check: the record's latitude and longitude are about 60 m from the Coast Guard's position (43 23 24.0 N, 065 37 16.9 W); no correction is proposed. The 1924 'built' date in the record is confirmed by the 1923-24 Marine report. Fact-check 2026-10-27: the story's 30 m height is now footnoted to the Coast Guard list (30.0 m) and the Directory (31 m) rather than to LighthouseFriends alone; the 1924 tower is given in metres first (26 m, 86 ft; 3 m, 10 ft); the LighthouseFriends details (1841 to 1924) were checked against its fetched page; the Marine entries for 1900, 1902, 1903, 1906, 1907 and 1924 were checked at their printed pages (p. 50, p. 76, p. 62, p. 38, p. 20, scan 54, p. 28) with corpus.py page; the Cass County Republican and Union and Journal pages (1860) were read directly. The 1907 diaphone entry is a fog-alarm inspection list whose printed page is not confirmed (scan page 54). The 1902 lens change (1 November 1902) is printed in the report for fiscal 1902, which was issued in 1903; the date is the report's own. The Lucille M sinking (25 July 1942) comes from uboat.net, while the station events of 26 July 1942 rest on LighthouseFriends' account of the Smith family's recollections.
